title: A performance refactor of AdminPermission.projects split one combined Q filter into chained .filter(teams__members=user).filter(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) calls, so read-only team members get admin rights on any project that also belongs to some admin team.

vulnerable_findings.explanation: In the both-flags-true branch, the PR removes the access-level filter entirely (`else: pass`), so `projects_from_teams` includes every team the user belongs to regardless of the team's `access` value. findings.explanation: In the both-flags-true branch, the PR removes the access-level filter entirely (`else: pass`), so `projects_from_teams` includes every team the user belongs to regardless of the team's `access` value. The base code always constrained the queryset to `teams__access` in {ADMIN_ACCESS, READ_ONLY_ACCESS}. Since `Team.access` is a non-enforced CharField (choices are advisory only), a team with any other `access` value now grants the user that project. This broadens the project set returned by `AdminPermission.projects(user, admin=True, member=True)`, which is used for admin-visibility checks (e.g. `RelatedProjectQuerySet._add_from_user_projects` and `AdminPermission.organizations`), so a user can be granted access to projects their team's access level should not authorize. This is an incorrect/broadened authorization condition.

evidence.content: You can create two types of teams: * Admin -- Team members have full access to administer the projects assigned to the team. ... * Read Only -- Team members are only able to read the documentation of each project, and not able to change anything about each project.

findings.suggested_fix: Do not drop the access filter when both flags are set. Keep the union of the two access levels, e.g. `projects_from_teams.filter(Q(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) | Q(teams__access=READ_ONLY_ACCESS))`, so only teams with a known, intended access level grant project access regardless of the combination of admin/member flags.
